questions.q: What is the primary physical property of components in a mixture that allows them to be separated by simple distillation?
questions.a: The primary property is a significant difference in their boiling points. A wrong answer—such as answering "solubility" or "magnetic susceptibility"—reveals a confusion with filtration, evaporation, or magnetic separation techniques where boiling points are irrelevant.

questions.q: During the distillation of a salt-water solution, why does pure water collect in the receiver flask while solid salt remains behind in the distilling flask?
questions.a: Water has a much lower boiling point than salt, so it vaporizes into steam when heated and then condenses back into liquid water in the condenser, whereas salt does not vaporize at that temperature. A student who thinks the salt also evaporates is confusing boiling points with melting points or sublimation.

questions.q: A laboratory mixture contains 100 mL of water (boiling point $100^\circ\text{C}$) and 100 mL of ethanol (boiling point $78.4^\circ\text{C}$). If you heat this mixture slowly, which substance will vaporize first, and what temperature will the thermometer first stabilize at?
questions.a: Ethanol will vaporize first because it has a lower boiling point, and the thermometer will stabilize at approximately $78.4^\circ\text{C}$ during its collection. A student who answers $100^\circ\text{C}$ fails to understand that the substance with the lower boiling point changes phase first before the mixture temperature can rise further.

questions.q: Why is running cold water in the outer jacket of a Liebig condenser made to flow upwards (from bottom to top) rather than downwards (from top to bottom)?
questions.a: Water flows upward to ensure the condenser jacket remains completely filled with cold water at all times, maximizing condensation efficiency. A wrong answer suggests the student views the condenser as a mere funnel rather than a heat-exchange jacket operating on counter-current cooling principles.

questions.q: Evaluate the safety of using simple distillation to separate a mixture of acetone (boiling point $56^\circ\text{C}$) and water ($100^\circ\text{C}$) using an open flame directly under the glass flask containing acetone. Why is this considered dangerous?
questions.a: Acetone is highly flammable; using an open flame directly beneath it creates a serious fire hazard if vapors escape or the flask cracks. A student who claims it is safe demonstrates a lack of awareness regarding the chemical properties (flammability) of organic solvents and the need for water baths or heating mantles.

questions.q: Design a modified distillation setup to obtain pure drinking water from muddy seawater. Which two separation techniques would you combine, and in what order?
questions.a: First, use filtration or sedimentation to remove insoluble mud particles, followed by simple distillation to remove dissolved salts from the filtrate. A poor answer fails to separate suspended solids before distillation, which would clog or contaminate the distillation flask.
